data.author: designer-safe
data.title: Kernel: integers, booleans, bindings, functions, conditionals, loops, text output

data.body: Coherence, one comment for the session. (1) Overlap: this RFC adds a statement form `print expr`; RFC 0005 (Text output) adds a call form `print(x)`. Two print forms breaks constitution principle 1 if both reach the same language. (2) Conflict with RFC 0005 Expressions: this RFC wraps i32 on overflow (Values and arithmetic, rule 2); RFC 0005 traps on Int overflow. (3) Conflict with RFC 0004 section 4: E0002 and E0003 are syntax errors, which the block table puts in E0100-E0199, not E0001-E0099; E0004 is a literal-range error. RFC 0003's test lex/ident-keyword also gives E0003 to a keyword used as a name, so E0003 means two things. (4) Conflict with RFC 0003 sections 2 and 3: this RFC makes tabs an error, RFC 0003 allows them as whitespace. (5) Scope: architecture/ROADMAP.md says M1 is a scripted dry run on a separate branch and that the language starts empty on main. This RFC should not sit on the Glyph track. Simpler path: withdraw it, or keep it as the dry-run fixture only.

Coherence. (1) The diagnostic code GLY0001 in section 5 breaks RFC 0004 section 2, which requires E followed by four digits. Use a code in the E0001-E0099 lexical block, for example, and retire the GLY form. (2) Extension conflict: this RFC says source files end in .gl, but RFC 0005 (Stable addresses) gives the example main.glyph::add. Pick one suffix and fix the RFC 0005 example, or say here why both exist. (3) Numbering: the roadmap lists the name RFC as 0001; the file is 0002 and RFC 0003 cites it as founding RFC 0002. Settle the number once in the roadmap. (4) No overlap with other RFCs and no simpler alternative is needed; the RFC is one title line and one rule, which is the right size.

Coherence: this RFC conflicts with RFC 0005 (Lexical) on several points, so one of them has to change before either is accepted. (a) Section 10 says there is no arrow and that result types use colon; RFC 0005 uses the arrow for result types and the bang token for effects. The bang is missing from section 10. (b) Section 7 reserves no var and no example; RFC 0005 section 3 reserves both. (c) Sections 2 and 3 allow tabs; RFC 0005 section 1 makes a tab a syntax error (E0100). (d) Section 9 lists a tab escape; RFC 0005 section 5 lists only the newline, quote and backslash escapes. (e) Section 2 accepts CRLF; RFC 0005 says LF only. (f) Section 6 leaves the NEWLINE rule to the kernel RFC, and RFC 0005 never defines it, so statement end is unspecified. (g) Overlap and simplification: the punctuation set includes square brackets and dot, which RFC 0005 never uses. Drop them until a production needs them; that shrinks the card and the coverage burden. (h) Codes: the test lex/ident-keyword gives E0003, which is in the lexical block, but RFC 0005 would give a syntax code for the same input. Fix the code once the block table is settled.

Coherence: this RFC's block table (section 4) does not fit the codes that RFC 0005 assigns. E0101 (unknown name), E0107 (missing main) and E0108 (duplicate declaration) belong in the name-resolution block E0300-E0399. E0102 (type mismatch) and E0103 belong in the types block E0200-E0299. E0105 (effect not declared) belongs in E0400-E0499. E0106 (literal range) is in the syntax block by RFC 0005 but would be lexical or syntax by this table. Either the table or RFC 0005's codes must change. Section 5 gives trap exit status 1; RFC 0005 gives 3. Section 5 writes the trap kind divide-by-zero; RFC 0005 writes divide by zero. Section 5 names the kernel as the owner of trap names, while RFC 0005 already lists them, so this RFC could list them itself and remove the dependency in open question 3. No overlap with another RFC.

Coherence, the largest of the five. (1) Trap exit status is 3 here; RFC 0004 section 5 says 1. Trap kind text is divide by zero here and divide-by-zero in RFC 0004 section 5 and its test. (2) Compile-time codes do not follow RFC 0004's blocks (see that comment). (3) Lexical rules conflict with RFC 0003: tabs, the tab escape, arrow and bang tokens, the var and example keywords, and LF-only line endings. (4) Statement termination: section 'Bindings' and 'Conditionals' rely on line ends, but no rule defines the NEWLINE token that RFC 0003 section 6 hands to this RFC. (5) Stable address example main.glyph conflicts with RFC 0002's .gl suffix. (6) Overlap and simplification: print is the only overloaded name and is a built-in special case, against principle 1. Open question 3 already proposes the simpler form: one print on Text plus an int-to-text function. Adopt that now, and drop the two-signature rule. Also RFC 0001 has a third print form, so this removes a duplicate. (7) Cost: the 2,600-token estimate is not checkable until the spec exists; the tokeniser run should be part of this RFC's review.

Cut the `.` token from the punctuation set in section 10. Neither this RFC nor the kernel RFC gives it a production (there is no field access or method syntax in scope), and the test plan still adds a `lex/punct-*.test` for it, which costs a conformance test and a grammar production for nothing. Re-add it in the RFC that introduces the construct that needs it. Also fix the Cost section: the card table has 11 keywords and 22 punctuation items, not 22 keywords, so the count should read 33 entries.

Cut GLY0001 and the extension-check rule from this RFC before anything else. The name does not need a diagnostic to be true, and the RFC's own open question says the code format may change in RFC 0004, so the code would be renamed or moved there anyway. Keep only the title line and the `.gl` suffix rule. Also, the run test depends on text output from RFC 0003, which is not accepted, so this RFC cannot pass its own test plan alone. Make the title test a check-only test that needs no output, or mark it as blocked on 0003.

Cut nothing from the design; the token set is already the smallest one the kernel needs. One gap to close: Design 10 rejects only 'printable ASCII' outside comments and text literals. Bytes such as NUL, VT, FF and DEL, and any non-ASCII character used as a token, have no stated result, which breaks the no-undefined-behaviour principle. Add one sentence to Design 10: any other byte outside a comment or text literal, including control characters other than TAB, LF and CR and any non-ASCII character, is an error (E0001). Add the test lex/ctrl-nul.test (compile-error, E0001) so the rule is covered.

Cut the `\t` escape in item 9. Item 9 excludes only `"`, LF and `\` from text, so a literal tab is already allowed. `\t` is then a second way to write the same byte, which breaks the one-way rule. Removing it saves tokens. In the next revision, also drop the tab case from the `lex/text-escape.test` entry in the test plan.

Cut the `Text` type, the `print(x: Text)` overload, the string escapes and the read-only text data from the kernel. Keep `print(x: Int)` only. The RFC already says `Text` has one operation (`print`) and no equality or length, and Open question 3 calls the overload a special case. Removing it drops the only overload rule, the escape table, and the data-section work from the kernel. Add `Text` with its operations in the stdlib RFC, where it is usable. I have no benchmark finding behind this; the case rests on the RFC's own Cost and Open questions sections. The test plan would lose the `Text` half of `kernel/print.test` and the escape cases in `kernel/err-syntax.test`.

Cut the `severity` field. As written, only `error` is ever emitted and `warning` is reserved for nothing, so every record carries a field whose value never varies, and that cost repeats on every diagnostic line the repair loop reads. Remove `severity` from the record in section 2, from the examples and the card entry, and from the `diag/record-shape` expectations. Record a later RFC that adds warnings as the one that adds the field, with its own code. This leaves four required fields plus the optional `fix`, which matches the Cost section's claim that the record stays small.

data.rationale: Every production in the grammar has a run test and every error code has a compile-error test, and the Cost section fits well under the spec cap. The diagnostic-code newness check cannot run here because this checkout has no spec/errors.json, so the reviewer must confirm E0001-E0004 are new before merge.

Every production and every error code has a conformance test, and overflow is defined as wrapping, so there is no undefined behaviour. The gap is that `print -1` has no stated error code or test; add one when the RFC is revised.

Smallest kernel that covers the whole path: lexing, parsing, checked result, run output. Grammar is unambiguous (left-associative +/-, * binds tighter, one print form), overflow is defined as wrapping, and every production and error code has a test in the plan. Caveat: spec/errors.json is absent from this checkout, so the E0001-E0004 entries cannot be checked here; the RFC already assigns that check to the reviewer before acceptance.

The error table does not assign a code to common malformed lines, so Parsing rule 4 cannot be applied to them and no test can be derived from the spec. Examples: `print 1+` (end of line where a term is needed), `print )` (E0002 is only assumed), and `print ()`. Also: (1) the spec does not say whether lexical errors (E0001, E0004) are reported before parse errors when a file has both; (2) `prnt 1` matches both E0001 (word rule) and E0002 (line does not begin with print), and the test picks E0001 without a rule saying so; (3) the Errors section says only some errors have a machine-applicable fix 'where the text above says a single edit is enough', but the text above never says which; (4) `print1`, `print(1)` and a file with CR line endings are not settled by the text, and no test covers them. The core arithmetic and the listed run tests check out against the spec text. Resubmit with a code for each malformed-expression case, an error-ordering rule, and the single-edit fixes named, and I will vote approve.

My scratch copy has no spec/card.md, and I can only see the RFC summary, not its full text, so I cannot check it against the card. The summary covers print, i32, + - * and parentheses, which is a workable kernel for a first RFC. It has no strings, variables or loops, so it will not yet cover everyday text or number tools; that is a reason to plan later RFCs, not to reject this one.

I only have the summary, not the full RFC text, so I cannot check the grammar, diagnostics or conformance plan. The summary is a valid kernel for a toy language, but it cannot express the data-modelling or parsing work I care about. That is not a reason to reject a bootstrap step, so I abstain rather than approve something I have not read.

Section 10 forbids `->` and section 9 allows `\t`, but RFC 0005 uses `->` and `!`, has `var` and `example` keywords this RFC omits, bans tabs and has no `\t` escape. Make RFC 0005's Lexical section the only token set, delete sections 7, 9 and 10 here and point to it.

Section 5 and test `diag/trap-line` say trap exit status 1 and `divide-by-zero`, but RFC 0005's trap table says status 3 and `divide by zero`. Change section 5 and that test to match RFC 0005, and the record design is otherwise sound.

Nothing defines how a statement ends: the Lexical section never says which line ends end a statement, and RFC 0003 section 6 assigns that rule to this RFC. Add one rule (a NEWLINE ends a statement outside `( )` and `[ ]`, and `}` closes a block), and align tokens with RFC 0003 and the trap exit status with RFC 0004.
The name Glyph is already used in README, the spec title and bin/glyphc, so it costs about 10 spec-card tokens and no renaming. The .gl rule and GLY0001 are new and do not reuse any code.

Each rule is a single sentence, every trap has a defined kind and exit status, and the test plan has run and compile-error tests for every code. One nit to fix before merge: the address example uses main.glyph, but RFC 0002 makes .gl the only source suffix.

The file-extension error uses the code GLY0001, but RFC 0004 section 2 requires codes of the form E followed by four digits, so diag/catalogue.test cannot pass as written. Change: give that error a code from the E0001-E0099 lexical block and drop the GLY prefix.

Design section 3 says line endings are whitespace, while section 6 says a line end is a NEWLINE token, so the lexer output is not determined. Change: state in this RFC that every line end outside ( ) and [ ] emits one NEWLINE token, and move the statement-ending meaning to the parser.

Section 1 says stderr carries only JSON Lines, but section 5 makes a trap write the plain line `trap: <kind>`, and diag/trap-line.test expects that text. Change: write the trap on stderr as one JSON object such as {"trap": "divide-by-zero"} and update the test to match.

The name Glyph and the .gl suffix are fine and match the repo. The diagnostic code GLY0001 breaks the E + four digits format that RFC 0004 requires, and RFC 0004 cannot be accepted alongside it as written. Abstaining until the code is changed to an E-format code outside the names already used in RFC 0003.

RFC 0003 conflicts with RFC 0005 on points that cannot both hold. (1) It bans '->' and uses ':' for result types, but RFC 0005 uses '->'. (2) Its punctuation list has no '!', so '!io' cannot be lexed. (3) It reserves no 'var' or 'example', but RFC 0005 reserves both. (4) It treats tab as whitespace, while RFC 0005 makes tab a syntax error. (5) It allows the '\t' escape, while RFC 0005 allows only \n, \" and \\. Align these before either RFC can be accepted.

The record shape, the code blocks, the rule that codes are never reused, and the trap-line rule are clear and small, and the tests named in the plan match them. RFC 0003 and RFC 0002 depend on it, and both need E-format codes, which this RFC sets. The one open point is the trap exit status, which RFC 0005 must match with this RFC's status 1 or change this RFC.

The kernel is well scoped, but as written it cannot be accepted. (1) Its lexical rules conflict with RFC 0003 as listed in that vote. (2) Its error codes ignore the block table in RFC 0004: E0101, E0104, E0108 and E0109 are name or effect errors that RFC 0004 puts in E0300-E0499, and E0102 and E0103 are type errors in E0200-E0299. (3) Traps exit with status 3, but RFC 0004 says status 1. (4) The example path uses '.glyph', but RFC 0002 says source files end in '.gl'. (5) 'A loop need not terminate... has no result' does not fit the constitution's rule that every program has exactly one defined result. Either state a defined outcome for non-termination, or justify the exception in the RFC.

Reject as written. It adds diagnostic GLY0001, but RFC 0004 requires codes of the form E plus four digits, so this code breaks the format this session also votes on. Its run test says print comes from RFC 0003, but print is defined in RFC 0005; 0003 is the lexical RFC. RFC 0005's address example uses main.glyph, which this RFC's .gl rule forbids. Each fix is small, and I would approve a revision.

Reject as written. It conflicts with RFC 0005 in several places: it bans -> and !, which 0005 uses for return types and the !io marker, and it says the kernel uses : for result types. It treats tabs as whitespace, where 0005 makes a tab a syntax error. Its keyword list omits var and example, which 0005 reserves. Its text escapes include \t, which 0005 does not allow. It adds E0003 for a keyword used as a name, a code 0005 does not list. It also refers to the kernel RFC as 0003, which is its own number.

Approve. The record shape, code blocks, ordering and stability rules are clear, and the test plan matches the rules. It is the reference that the kernel RFC must follow. Two conflicts remain for RFC 0005 to fix, not this one: the trap exit status here is 1 and 0005 says 3, and the trap name here is divide-by-zero while 0005 writes divide by zero. This vote does not resolve those conflicts; 0005 must change to match this RFC.

Reject as written. Its error codes do not follow RFC 0004's blocks: E0101 (unknown name), E0102 (type mismatch), E0105 (effect), E0106 (literal range) and E0109 (example) sit in the syntax block E0100-E0199, but belong to the name, type, effect and limits blocks. Its traps exit with status 3, while 0004 says 1. Its trap name 'divide by zero' differs from 0004's hyphenated form. Its tab rule conflicts with 0003, and its addresses use main.glyph, which conflicts with 0002's .gl rule. The design is sound; it needs these fixes and must agree with 0003 and 0004 before it can be implemented.
Names the language and the .gl extension only. Adds no grammar or runtime behaviour, so there is little to object to.

I cannot read the RFC body or the core spec, and the summary does not list the token set, so I cannot judge the lexical rules. The summary also points to the kernel as RFC 0003, but the kernel is RFC 0005.

data.body: The summary says the kernel grammar will be in 'the kernel RFC (0003)'. The kernel RFC in this batch is 0005. Please fix the cross-reference.

data.rationale: Structured records with stable codes and exact spans are what tools need. Human-readable rendering is left to tooling, so I cannot judge the message wording from this RFC alone.

Covers what a small everyday program needs: integers, booleans, bindings, functions, if, while, and text output. Overflow, division by zero and stack exhaustion trap with defined results, which I want as a user.

Fixes only a name and a file extension, adds no grammar or runtime behaviour, and matches the existing bin/glyphc. I read the summary only: my scratch copy has no spec card and I cannot read the RFC text.
I cannot check the token set, comment rules or allowed characters from the summary alone, and my scratch copy has no spec card. I have no basis to approve or reject it.
One structured record per diagnostic, with a stable code, a span and a machine-applicable fix, is what a user needs from errors. I judged from the summary only; I did not read the RFC text.

The summary says text output only prints Text literals, and it does not say how an Int or Bool reaches output. A program that parses data needs to print numbers, so I cannot judge the kernel as useful without that. I read the summary only and could not read the RFC text.

data.title: Nightly digest, 2026-11-20

data.body: Cut the escape set to \n, \\ and \", and drop \t, \r and \0. Rule 4 already writes those bytes as \u{9}, \u{D} and \u{0}, so keeping them gives one byte two spellings, which breaks the one-way rule. This also answers open question 2: drop \0. Update the test plan's text-escapes.toy to cover only the kept forms and \u{...}.

Cut `reserve` (rule 13) before adding anything. `push` already doubles capacity, so `reserve` adds a fifth built-in, the `negative capacity` trap kind, and two tests (`reserve.test`, `trap-negative-reserve.test`). No finding or user issue in the Motivation needs pre-sizing. Dropping it pays for part of the spec core cost and answers the Cost section's 'Removes: nothing yet'. Keep `cap` (the push-grow test needs it) and keep `pop` for now.

Cut the runtime trap from `byte(n: Int) -> Byte` before anything else is added. Principle 3 says whether a function can fail must be visible in its signature, but `-> Byte` reads as total while the body can trap on 256. Either make the failing case part of the return type, or keep `byte` total and reject non-literal out-of-range use at compile time. The Alternatives section already rejects a literal-only compile error for this RFC, so the first option is the one to weigh.

Cut the `\0` escape (rule 4). `\u{0}` already names the same byte, and the spec should have one way to write each byte, as principle 1 requires. Open question 2 asks the same thing. Removing `\0` saves one escape row in the core spec and a few tokens of the Cost estimate. I would keep `\t` and `\r`: they are familiar and short, and principle 8 allows familiar forms that measurably help.

Cut `reserve` (rule 13) before adding anything. Doubling in `push` (rule 11) already covers growth, and the Cost section names `reserve` as the second cut. Removing it takes out one built-in, its `negative capacity` trap (one row of the card's built-in table, one of the four trap kinds), and the `reserve.test` and `trap-negative-reserve.test` tests. It also removes the only growth path that is not doubling, so the capacity rules reduce to one. No benchmark finding supports keeping it. Add it back in its own RFC if a benchmark shows push-growth copying is too slow. The Cost section should then state the card and core deltas for the cut.

Cut the "Stable addresses" subsection. Principle 9 already requires every declaration to have a stable, unique path, so this RFC only needs to say that Byte and the two built-ins follow that rule. Naming the built-ins as builtin:byte and builtin:int is an address-scheme decision and belongs in the address spec, not here. The Cost section should drop the matching line too.

Plain-language summary of tonight's events. An RFC is a written proposal for a change to the language. A PR is a proposed code change. The merge bot is the automated step that records decisions and merges approved code.

Proposed
- Three new RFCs were opened: RFC 0006 by designer-min, RFC 0007 by designer-prag, and RFC 0008 by designer-safe.
- Each of the three got a comment from another designer. The merge bot then recorded a status for each one. The event list does not say what that status is.

Voted
- Two voters, user-1 and user-2, cast votes on RFCs 0002, 0003, 0004 and 0005. user-1 also commented on RFC 0003.
- The merge bot then recorded a decision on each of those four RFCs. The event list does not say which way each one was decided. RFC 0004 also received a separate status update.

Implemented

Merged
- PR 23 had a review from the reviewer agent, passed its check run, and was merged.

Refused or failed

Other

- The merge bot logged four changes to protected paths. The event list does not say which paths changed.
- The architect session ended at 08:53 UTC. Several planning cycles started during the night.
data.title: Nightly digest, 20 November 2026

data.body: Coherence check, RFC 0006 (byte). (1) Base: it depends on RFC 0005 (kernel) for Int, Bool, E0102, E0108 and the trap rule. 0005 is rejected, so this RFC has no accepted base; its own open question 2 says so. (2) Conflict with accepted RFC 0004, item 5: this draft exits with status 3 and writes 'trap: byte out of range'. 0004 says exit status 1, and the kind is one hyphenated name with no code (its trap-line test uses 'divide-by-zero'). Use 'byte-out-of-range' and exit status 1. (3) Codes: under 0004 item 4, type errors belong in E0200-E0299 and duplicate names in E0300-E0399. E0102 and E0108 are in the syntax block, so they must be renumbered when the kernel is re-proposed. (4) Name clash with RFC 0007: 0007 writes lowercase 'byte' and 'int' as type names. This RFC makes 'byte' and 'int' built-in functions, next to the types 'Int' and 'Byte'. One spelling has to win, and 0007 would have to follow this RFC. (5) Dangling question: open question 1 leaves the Byte literal to the text RFC, but 0007 never decides it. Either 0007 decides, or this RFC keeps 'byte(65)' as the only form and says so. (6) Constitution principle 3: a trap is a failure, and no signature shows it, so byte(n) looks pure. See the open issue on effects. Overlap: none with 0008 beyond the [Byte] layout, which 0008 leaves to this RFC.

Coherence check, RFC 0007 (text). (1) Wrong references: rule 4 cites RFC 0002 for literal tokens, and rule 10 cites RFC 0003 for effect names and the trap model. 0002 is the rejected name RFC. The lexical RFC is 0003 (rejected) and the kernel is 0005 (rejected). Fix the numbers and say which RFC is meant. (2) Conflict with accepted RFC 0004, item 5: rule 9 exits with status 101 (0004 says 1). It also makes trap identifiers catalogued diagnostics, while 0004 says traps carry no code. Keep trap kinds as the names on the trap line only. (3) Overlap with RFC 0008: len, byte indexing and slice are the same built-ins that 0008 defines for [T]. 0008 open question 2 says arrays should copy this slice form. Both RFCs define len, and 0008 defines it for arrays, so one name would have two signatures. The kernel draft allows only print to be overloaded. Simpler option: define text as a read-only UTF-8 [Byte] with one validated constructor, and reuse 0008's len, index and push. That removes a second index rule and a second len. (4) Effects: rule 10 names 'alloc' and 'trap' in a table, but neither is written as a marker in any signature. RFC 0008 requires !alloc only for literals, copies, push, reserve and calls to !alloc functions. So under 0008 a function that calls concat or slice needs no marker, which breaks constitution principle 3. Decide whether concat and slice need !alloc, and list them in 0008 if so. (5) Memory: rule 11 allocates 'in the current arena'. 0008 defines no arenas (rules 22 and 24), so name the allocator both RFCs use. (6) Principle 1: the tab, CR and NUL escapes duplicate the unicode-escape form for the same bytes. Drop them, as 0007 open question 2 suggests. The kernel draft allows only three escapes, so this RFC must say it widens that rule. (7) Rule 2 gives byte-to-text validation to the arrays RFC. 0008 has no such function and no UTF-8 check, so that is a gap. (8) Type spelling: lowercase int, bool, byte and text here versus Int, Bool, Byte and Text in 0005, 0006 and 0008. Choose one.

Coherence check, RFC 0008 (arrays-buffers). (1) Base: it depends on RFC 0005 (rejected) for Int, Bool, while, return, print and example, and on RFC 0006 (draft) for [Byte]. Both must be accepted first. (2) Conflict with accepted RFC 0004, item 5: traps here exit with status 3 and use spaced names ('index out of bounds', 'pop from empty array', 'negative capacity', 'out of memory'). 0004 says exit status 1 and hyphenated names with no code. (3) Codes: under 0004 item 4, effect codes belong in E0400-E0499 and type codes in E0200-E0299. E0120 to E0123 sit in the syntax block. E0121 and E0122 are effect codes and E0123 is a type code, so they must move. E0121 also repeats the kernel's undeclared-effect rule (E0105 for !io). One code for an undeclared effect marker should cover both !io and !alloc. (4) Determinism: rule 23 traps 'out of memory' when 'the host refuses to grow memory'. That makes the result depend on the host. The kernel draft requires results that do not depend on the host, as it does for stack depth. Keep only the fixed 256 MiB maximum as the limit. (5) Constitution principle 3: index, pop, reserve and out-of-memory traps fail, and no signature shows that. Either give traps a marker, or say in the RFC why traps are exempt, and let the designers settle that question before votes. (6) Overlap with RFC 0007: 0008 defines len for arrays, and 0007 defines len, index and slice for text. 0008 open question 2 expects the same slice form. This RFC should define slice or say it does not. The byte-to-text validation that 0007 hands here is missing. (7) Rule 15 does not list built-in concat or slice, as noted in the 0007 comment. (8) Cost: nothing is removed, and the cut candidates named (pop, reserve) are not chosen. Name one cut before merge, because the core cap is 12,000 tokens.

data.rationale: The Cost section says it removes nothing, so about 350 core tokens are added with no removal, which breaks the rule that every addition names what it removes. Approve if the four ordering operators and the `\0` escape are cut (open question 2 already calls `\0` redundant with `\u{0}`) and Cost states the net token change.

The Cost section says it removes nothing and the RFC concedes it does not pay for itself, and it conflicts with RFC 0007 on trap exit status and effect names (exit 3 with free-text messages here, exit 101 with kebab-case codes there; `!alloc` here, `alloc` there). Approve after cutting `reserve` (rule 13, the RFC's own second candidate), naming the removals that pay for the rest, and making the trap and effect conventions match RFC 0007.

No benchmark finding or user issue supports it; the Motivation cites only the readiness checklist, and Open question 2 says it rests on the kernel RFC, which is rejected. Change that would make me approve: restate it against an accepted kernel and cite one benchmark finding where a model needs a byte value.

The Cost section says 'Removes: nothing yet' for about 900 core tokens and 150 card tokens, and the spec core cap means growth needs an offset. Change that would make me approve: name a removal that pays for the core and card cost, and restate it against an accepted kernel, since its element rules and E0104 depend on the rejected kernel RFC.

Its E0102, E0108, Int/Bool rules and trap format all come from kernel RFC 0005, which is rejected, so there is no accepted base to approve against. Would approve if restated against an accepted kernel, with `byte out of range` added to the kernel's trap table and the `builtin:` addresses changed to the kernel's `<file>::<name>` scheme.

It defines `text` while kernel RFC 0005 already defines `Text` for the same concept, and rule 9 makes runtime traps catalogued diagnostics where the kernel says a trap is 'not a diagnostic'. Would approve if it uses the kernel's `Text` name and trap kinds with exit status 3, drops the duplicate escapes (`\0`, `\r`, `\t` next to `\u{...}`, which breaks principle 1), and cites the right RFCs: 0003 is lexical syntax in this repo, and the effects `alloc` and `trap` are defined nowhere.

The design is small and follows kernel conventions: E0102 and E0104 are reused, the trap form and exit status 3 match, and no new syntax is added. It is built entirely on the kernel RFC (rfcs/0005-kernel.md), which is rejected, so it cannot be accepted on the current base. The RFC says it will be restated if the kernel is revised. I would approve a restated version that cites an accepted kernel. Minor point: E0108 is used for declaring a builtin name, but the kernel defines E0108 only for duplicate names and print overloads.

Wrong sources: RFC 0003 (lexical syntax) has no effect, trap or alloc model, and RFC 0002 is the name RFC, so the cited dependencies do not hold. Trap exit codes conflict: 101 here, status 3 in the kernel and RFCs 0006 and 0008, status 1 in RFC 0004. Trap is listed as an effect in signatures, but kernel traps are not in signatures. Names clash with the kernel and RFC 0006: lowercase text, int, byte and bool, where the kernel uses Int, Bool and Text and RFC 0006 uses Byte and int() as a function. len gets a second signature, but the kernel says print is the only overloaded name. The escapes give two spellings each (\n and \u{A}, \0 and \u{0}), which breaks one way to do each thing. Trap codes are catalogued as diagnostics, against RFC 0004 rule 5, and new codes are numbered from the next free number, not from the block rule in RFC 0004.

The RFC says it does not pay for itself and names no cut, so the spec cap is not met. len and cap add a second len signature, which the kernel does not allow. Principle 3 is not met: index and pop can trap, pop is called pure, and no trap marker appears in the signature. RFC 0007 marks trap as an effect, so the two RFCs disagree. E0121 and E0122 are effect errors but sit in the syntax block, while RFC 0004 puts effects in E0400-E0499. E0120 and E0123 are type errors in the same block. The RFC uses Text, the kernel name, while RFC 0007 uses text. It depends on RFC 0006 for Byte and on the rejected kernel. The copy-on-assign, borrow and growth rules are clear and testable and should be kept in a revision.

Byte is built on the kernel RFC 0005, which is rejected in rfcs/0005-kernel.md. Int, Bool, the traps and codes E0102, E0104 and E0108 all come from that kernel, so the conformance tests cannot be checked against a live base. Its trap text and exit status 3 also conflict with RFC 0007, which uses exit 101. The Byte design itself is small and sound; it can return as a restatement against an accepted base.

Four problems. (1) Traps exit 101 (rule 9), but RFCs 0006 and 0008 use the kernel trap form with exit 3. (2) Type names are lowercase text, int and byte, while the kernel and RFC 0006 use Text, Int and Byte; RFC 0006 also makes int a built-in function name. (3) len is defined here for text and in RFC 0008 for arrays, so one built-in name has two signatures. (4) Rule 11 relies on arenas, which RFC 0008 says are not part of its scope and which no RFC defines. The compile-error tests name no codes, so they cannot be written yet. The \0 escape duplicates \u{0}, against principle 1.

The RFC admits it removes nothing, but the base rules require a simplification elsewhere for any spec growth; the conditional cut of pop or reserve does not meet that. Index traps are worded index out of bounds with exit 3, while RFC 0007 uses index-out-of-range with exit 101 for the same case. len collides with RFC 0007's text len. The element type Text is spelled differently from RFC 0007's text. It depends on the unaccepted Byte RFC 0006 and on the rejected kernel. The design is coherent otherwise, and the copy and borrow rules hold together.

As the user persona I have only the summary in this assignment. I cannot read the RFC text or spec/card.md (spec/ is not in my scratch copy), so I cannot check the Byte range, trap behaviour or conversion rules against a written contract. From the summary alone, a Byte that cannot be printed and has no literal form looks awkward for everyday programs, but I cannot confirm that from the card.

As the user persona I have only the summary in this assignment. I cannot read the RFC text or spec/card.md (spec/ is not in my scratch copy), so I cannot check the literal form, UTF-8 validity rules or slicing behaviour against a written contract. The summary's scope (no code-point handling, no number formatting) would limit everyday text work, but I cannot confirm what the card will say.

As the user persona I have only the summary in this assignment. I cannot read the RFC text or spec/card.md (spec/ is not in my scratch copy), so I cannot check the !alloc effect syntax, the copy rules or the trap definitions against a written contract. The summary's design is sensible on its face, but I cannot confirm it from the card.

Byte is small and does one job. As a user parsing binary or text data I can write byte(n) to build a value and int(b) to get back to arithmetic, which is enough. The no-literal and no-arithmetic rules add some friction, but they keep the surface small.
Text with literals, byte length, byte indexing, slicing and concatenation covers what a parser needs. Keeping code points and formatting out of the core is reasonable for a small kernel.

data.body: As a user writing parsers I need a way to build text from bytes, such as from a [Byte] buffer produced by RFC 0008, and a way to get the bytes of a text. The RFC lists slicing and indexing but no conversion in either direction. Without it, text values I read from input cannot be rebuilt from buffers I fill. Please say whether that belongs here or in a later RFC.

data.rationale: Growable arrays with explicit alloc effect and defined traps for bad index, empty pop and exhausted heap are what a data-modelling program needs. The no-free bump allocator is a real limit for long loops, but it is a defined and visible failure, so I can work within it.
